claimText: Under section 330 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, the failure-to-disclose offence is triggered by knowledge, suspicion, or reasonable grounds for knowing or suspecting money laundering, based on the regulated person's own information, a self-contained, negligence-style trigger per legislation.gov.uk's own Explanatory Notes to subsection (2)(b), independent of whether another institution has separately reported or discovered anything.

source.title: Proceeds of Crime Act 2002, Section 330 and Explanatory Notes

claimText: Corroborating legal commentary supporting the reading that section 330's trigger depends on information that actually came to the regulated person in the course of their own business, a self-contained standard not dependent on coordination between institutions.

source.title: Will the CPS' decision to update its guidance mean an increase in prosecutions for failure to disclose under section 330 of POCA 2002?
source.publisher: Kingsley Napley LLP, Criminal Law Blog

claimText: Sections 339ZB to 339ZD of POCA 2002, inserted by section 11 of the Criminal Finances Act 2017, create a voluntary information-sharing gateway between regulated-sector institutions for suspected money laundering, subject to conditions (an affirmative request from the recipient or the NCA, prior NCA notification), not an automatic mechanism, and can lead to a joint disclosure report to the NCA (a 'Super SAR') that can itself satisfy the section 330 reporting requirement.

source.title: Criminal Finances Act 2017, Explanatory Notes, Division 6 (paras. 101-104)

claimText: Section 339A POCA 2002 exempts two specific circumstances from needing a Defence Against Money Laundering before proceeding, not a general low-value-transaction allowance: a deposit-taking body, e-money institution, or payment institution operating an account below the threshold (subsection 2), and a regulated-sector person paying away property when terminating a business relationship (subsection 6A). Both thresholds are currently £3,000, raised from £1,000 on 31 July 2025 by SI 2025/877, itself raised from £250 on 5 January 2023, two separate increases.

source.title: The Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) (Threshold Amount) (Amendment) Order 2025 (SI 2025/877)

claimText: The default match-score threshold for OpenSanctions-backed screening (above which a candidate is surfaced as a match) is 0.7, and the default algorithm is calibrated to be used with that value.

source.title: OpenSanctions API: Tuning the Matching System

claimText: A match query is processed in two stages: first a search index locates candidate results optimized for recall (retrieval), then those candidates are evaluated against the query using the configured matching algorithm (scoring).

source.title: OpenSanctions API: Tuning the Matching System

claimText: OpenSanctions' regression-v1 matching algorithm scores candidates across exactly 18 named features (e.g. name_match, name_token_overlap, name_levenshtein, dob_matches, dob_year_matches, dob_year_disjoint, identifier_match, org_identifier_match, address_match, gender_mismatch, country_mismatch, and others), confirmed by manual count of the published feature table, not name similarity alone.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: Supported Matching Algorithms

claimText: The name-based and name-qualified algorithms compare names using Jaro-Winkler string similarity combined with Soundex phonetic matching, are both deprecated in favour of the ofac (OFACMatcher) algorithm, and OpenSanctions' own documentation states neither reaches parity with OFAC's public Sanctions List Search tool.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: Deprecated Matching Algorithms

claimText: A separate algorithm (ofac / OFACMatcher) is reverse-engineered from OFAC's own scoring FAQ (FAQ #249) and parity fixtures captured against the live public tool, specifically to emulate sanctionssearch.ofac.treas.gov's behaviour, distinct from the deprecated name-based and name-qualified algorithms.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher: ofac Algorithm

claimText: logic-v2 is a deterministic, rule-based matching algorithm whose name matcher uses curated, multilingual cultural reference data for cross-language and cross-script matching, and OpenSanctions' own API tuning documentation recommends pinning to logic-v2 for new integrations.

source.title: OpenSanctions Matcher (logic-v2) and API Tuning documentation

claimText: Two individuals named Khalid Mehmood on Pakistan's proscribed persons list, sharing the same name, country, and sanctions programme but different national ID numbers (ending 9885 and 0181) and different father's names (Muhammad Khan and Haji Muhammad), were assigned a 0.98 match score by a rule-based (RegressionV1/Nomenklatura) baseline in a February 2026 academic benchmark.

claimText: yente release v5.4.0 (13 May 2026) fixed a cross-script candidate-ranking bug: when a Latin-script candidate already carried the symbolic evidence of a same-script match, an Arabic/Cyrillic/etc. rendering of the same name could previously outrank it at the retrieval stage; the release aligned Elasticsearch candidate-fetch weighting with how the scoring stage already valued that evidence.

source.title: opensanctions/yente Release v5.4.0

claimText: An AI agent is software that can interpret a goal, break it into steps, and act on digital services with limited human input at each step, rather than requiring explicit approval for every action. claimText: FG25/3 (July 2025) confirms UK (domestic) PEPs are treated as lower risk than foreign PEPs as a starting point (Regulation 35(3A)). Non-executive board members of central government boards in the UK are not treated as PEPs (unless they separately meet the PEP definition in another capacity). Junior or mid-ranking civil servants are not treated as PEPs. Military officials are NOT categorically excluded: the guidance explicitly includes high-ranking officers in the armed forces as a PEP category, scoped to those at Permanent Secretary/Deputy Permanent Secretary-equivalent rank (Vice Admiral, Lieutenant General, or Air Marshal). A firm's MLRO need not personally sign off every PEP relationship provided a suitably senior person does so and the MLRO retains oversight. Firms must document their rationale where they apply continued EDD to a former PEP beyond the standard baseline (Regulation 35(9)(b)).

source.title: FG25/3: The treatment of politically exposed persons for anti-money laundering purposes

note: Real correction found and fixed during this sourcing pass, not just a citation add: the guide's original text stated 'military officials are NOT classified as PEPs' in two places (the 2026-changes callout and the FAQ). Checked against the FCA's own FG25/3 PDF (fetched directly, not a secondary summary): the guidance explicitly lists 'ambassadors, charges d'affaires and high-ranking officers in the armed forces' as a PEP category, scoped to Permanent Secretary-equivalent rank (Vice Admiral, Lieutenant General, or Air Marshal). Only junior/mid-ranking military personnel are excluded, the same threshold that excludes junior civil servants generally, not military officials as a category. Both occurrences reworded to state the accurate, narrower scope before citing, per the instruction not to cite an inaccurate paraphrase.

claimText: TA 2000 s.15 covers inviting or receiving money or property while intending, or having reasonable cause to suspect, that it may be used for terrorism, or providing it while knowing, or having reasonable cause to suspect, that it will or may be so used. S.17 covers entering into or becoming concerned in a funding arrangement while knowing or having reasonable cause to suspect the property will or may be used for terrorism. S.18 covers entering into or becoming concerned in an arrangement facilitating another person's retention or control of terrorist property; a defence is available where the person proves (conjunctively) that they did not know AND had no reasonable cause to suspect the arrangement related to terrorist property. Penalties are set out in s.22.

source.title: Terrorism Act 2000, Sections 15, 17, 18, and 22

note: Corrected twice on the same claim. Round 2 (this ledger entry's prior version) replaced loose paraphrases with wording that itself contained two further errors, caught by an external adversarial review, not this project's own checklist: (1) s.15 conflated the 'intending or reasonable cause to suspect' standard that applies to inviting/receiving with the narrower 'knowing or reasonable cause to suspect' standard that applies only to providing, presenting one unified standard where the statute actually sets two different ones for the two limbs of the offence; (2) s.18's defence was described as available if the person lacked knowledge OR reasonable cause to suspect (disjunctive, either limb sufficient), when s.18(2) actually requires the person to prove BOTH limbs conjunctively (no knowledge AND no reasonable cause to suspect) to make out the defence. Both fixed in this entry and in the guide's on-page text. s.16 description remains out of scope, per the original correction's own boundary.

claimText: The FCA's five-step penalty methodology under DEPP 6.5 is: (1) removal of financial benefit derived directly from the breach, (2) a figure reflecting the seriousness of the breach (relevant revenue for firms, relevant income for individuals), (3) adjustment for aggravating/mitigating factors, (4) upward adjustment for deterrence, (5) settlement discount (up to 30%, applied during Stage 1, not to the disgorgement step).
